entries.modern_form: PIE *eter- 'entrails, intestines' (Pokorny 344 = Walde-Pokorny I 117); the Iranian attachment (Av. xᵛāθra- < *hu-āθra-) is Pokorny's own tentative suggestion
entries.note: Pokorny p.344 has the lemma exactly: 'Root/lemma: eter-, Meaning: intestines', built on Gk. ἦτορ 'heart' (Aeolic for *etr̥), ἦτρον 'belly, lower abdomen', ON æðr 'vein', OE ǣdre, OHG ād(a)ra 'vein, sinew, pl. entrails', OHG innuodili, OIr. inathar 'entrails'. The root and the language label are right; the gloss is not. Nourai's 'internal (INSIGNIFICANT) organs' is his own addition, inserted so that the Persian 'of low value' can fall out of the root — no source glosses *eter- as 'insignificant'. The one Iranian link is the last line of Pokorny's article: 'from here Avestan xᵛāθra- "moments of joy, cheerfulness, contentment" as *su-atra-?' — offered with a question mark. Modern Iranian etymology (Rastorgujeva–Edelʹman, ESIJa I 324, quoted by Wiktionary) takes MP xwār back to PIr *āθra- and calls the further origin unknown, i.e. it neither adopts nor refutes Pokorny's *eter-. Watkins/AHD dropped the root altogether (no *eter- in the 1985 appendix). Verdict: plausible — real root, real forms, over-tailored gloss, and a weakly supported Iranian bridge. Two of the three references Nourai cites for the root do not check out (see ref_check).

nodes.derivation: All three shapes are one and the same Avestan compound. Av. xᵛāθra- n. = xᵛ- (hu-) 'good' + āθra-, and duž-āθra- = duš- 'bad' + āθra-; Nourai's 'su-âthra' is simply the Indic-looking spelling su- of the same prefix that appears as Iranian hu-/xᵛ-, which is why he can only gloss it '?'. Pokorny 344 takes the *-āθra- element as the reflex of *eter- 'entrails', so that *su-atra- is literally 'good-innards' > 'well-being' — the same figure as Latin viscera / Greek σπλάγχνα for the seat of feeling. The GLOSSES on the chart are wrong: Bartholomae's Altiranisches Wörterbuch gives xᵛāθra- 'Behagen, Glück, Wonne' (comfort, happiness) — see the compounds pouruš-xᵛāθra- 'der viel Behagen, Glück, Wonne gewährt' and vīspa-xᵛāθra- 'der alles Behagen … besitzt und gewährt' — and duž-āθra- is its antonym 'discomfort, distress'. 'Insignificant, low in value' is New Persian semantics read back into Avestan: the road runs 'comfortable' > 'easy' > 'trifling' > 'of no worth', and Horn (no.496) states flatly that the sense 'niedrig, verächtlich' is FIRST New Persian. So the node is right about the forms and about which Avestan words feed the Persian pair, and wrong about what those Avestan words mean.
nodes.derivation_fa: هر سه صورت در واقع یک واژه‌اند: اوستایی xᵛāθra- از پیشوند xᵛ-/hu- «خوب» + ستاک āθra-، و duž-āθra- از duš- «بد» + همان ستاک؛ «su-āthra» هم صورت هندی‌نمای همان پیشوند hu- است و از همین رو نورایی معنایی برایش نیاورده. پوکورنی جزء دوم را بازماندهٔ ریشهٔ *eter- «اندرونه» می‌داند، یعنی *hu-āθra- تحت‌اللفظ «خوش‌اندرون» و مجازاً «آسایش». امّا معنایی که در نمودار آمده درست نیست: بارتولومه xᵛāθra- را «Behagen, Glück» (آسایش، خوشی) معنی کرده و آن را در ترکیب‌های pouruš-xᵛāθra- و vīspa-xᵛāθra- آورده است، و duž-āθra- ضدّ آن است؛ معنی «کم‌ارزش، خوار» تحوّل معنایی متأخّرِ فارسی نو است — چنان‌که هرن (شمارهٔ ۴۹۶) صریحاً می‌گوید معنی «پست و خوارشمرده» تنها در فارسی نو پیدا شده است. پس صورت‌ها و مسیر درست‌اند، ولی معنای اوستایی در کتاب نادرست است: با احتیاط پذیرفتنی است.

nodes.derivation: Av. xᵛāθra- 'comfort' > MP xwār. The intervocalic -θr- of Old Iranian gives Middle Persian -hr-/-r- (cf. puθra- > pus(ar), miθra- > Mihr), so *xwāθra- > xwā(h)r, whence MacKenzie's two entries side by side: 'xwār [hwl] light, easy; mean, abject' with abstract xwārīh 'ease', and 'xwā(h)rīh [hw'(h)ryh, Man. xw'ryy] happiness, bliss' — the older abstract still carrying the Avestan 'well-being'. Nyberg's glossary has 'xᵛārēh [hw'lyh] bliss, felicity, delight — from ¹xᵛār' and 'a-xwārīh unhappiness'. For the negative: MP dušwār / duš-xwar 'difficult, disagreeable' (MacKenzie: 'dušwār [dwšw'l, Man. dwšw'r] difficult, disagreeable; ~īh difficulty, trouble'; 'duš-xwar = dušwār'), attested in Book Pahlavi (Nyberg quotes hac hān dušxᵛār sahist 'by this he was much shocked'). One refinement of Nourai's arrow: Horn no.569 says the Middle and New Persian forms are 'Neubildungen aus duš + xwār' — a fresh compound made on Iranian soil from the living prefix duš- and xwār, not a phonetic continuation of Av. dužāθra-; the Avestan word is the model, not the direct ancestor.
nodes.derivation_fa: اوستایی xᵛāθra- «آسایش» در فارسی میانه به xwār بدل شده است؛ خوشهٔ -θr- ایرانی باستان در میانِ واکه در پهلوی به -hr-/-r- دگرگون می‌شود (مانند puθra- > پسر، miθra- > مهر). مکنزی دو مدخل کنار هم دارد: «xwār سبک، آسان؛ پست، خوار» با نامِ مصدر xwārīh «آسانی»، و «xwā(h)rīh شادکامی، خوشی» که هنوز معنی اوستایی را نگاه داشته است. نیبرگ نیز xᵛārēh «خوشی، شادکامی» را از ¹xᵛār گرفته و a-xwārīh «ناخوشی» را آورده است. صورت منفی، پهلویِ dušwār / duš-xwar «سخت، دشوار» است (مکنزی؛ و نیبرگ شاهدِ hac hān dušxᵛār sahist را می‌آورد). یک نکتهٔ اصلاحی: هرن (شمارهٔ ۵۶۹) صورت‌های پهلوی و فارسی را «ساخت تازه» از duš + xwār می‌داند، نه دنبالهٔ آواییِ مستقیمِ اوستایی dužāθra-؛ یعنی واژهٔ اوستایی الگو بوده است نه نیای بی‌واسطه. ادعای نورایی درست است.

nodes.derivation: MP xwār > NP خوار xᵛār/xār. In New Persian the word keeps 'easy, light' (archaic) and develops the dominant modern sense 'contemptible, abject, of no worth' — Horn no.496 ends: 'Die Bedeutung "niedrig, verächtlich" ist erst neupersisch'; Wiktionary (after Rastorgujeva–Edelʹman ESIJa I 324) lists exactly these two senses, '(archaic) easy' and 'mean, abject', from MP xwār. MP dušxwār/dušwār > NP دشوار dušvār 'difficult'; the older دشخوار is still in the dictionaries beside it (Borhān has both headwords, and Moʿin's Farhang cross-refers 'دشوار … دشخوار'), the -šxw- cluster simplifying to -šv-. Ferdowsi already sets the pair against each other (Horn's footnote cites Šāhnāma I 170 v.745, 'np. xᵛār directly opposed to dušxᵛār, as in the Avesta xᵛāθra- to dužāθra-'). Moʿin's etymological footnote in Borhān-e Qāteʿ p.780 s.v. خوار reads 'اوستا xᵛāθra- (رفاه، آسایش) «خرده اوستا ۲۹۱»، پهلوی xᵛār، کردی xār، افغانی xwār، بلوچی xwār، طبری xār (خوب)' — i.e. exactly Nourai's chain, but glossing the Avestan word 'welfare, ease'. The box's own NOTE ('See root "Xwâr" for a different derivation') should be read the other way round: the derivation drawn HERE is the mainstream one (Horn, Hübschmann, Moʿin, MacKenzie, ESIJa); the alternative under Nourai's separate root Xwâr is the minority option.
nodes.derivation_fa: فارسی میانهٔ xwār در فارسی نو «خوار» شده است: معنی کهن «آسان، سبک» است و معنی رایج امروزی «پست، بی‌ارزش، خوارشمرده» — هرن در پایان شمارهٔ ۴۹۶ می‌نویسد که معنی «پست و خوار» تنها نوفارسی است، و ویکی‌واژه (به نقل از فرهنگ ریشه‌شناختی زبان‌های ایرانی ج۱ ص ۳۲۴) همین دو معنی را از پهلویِ xwār می‌گیرد. «دشوار» از پهلویِ dušxwār/dušwār است و صورت کهن‌تر «دشخوار» هنوز در فرهنگ‌ها کنار آن هست (برهان قاطع هر دو مدخل را دارد و معین در فرهنگ فارسی «دشوار … دشخوار» را برابر آورده)؛ خوشهٔ -شخو- به -شو- ساده شده است. فردوسی نیز «خوار» را در برابر «دشوار» می‌نهد (شاهنامه ج۱ ص ۱۷۰ بیت ۷۴۵، به نقل هرن). حاشیهٔ ریشه‌شناختی معین در برهان قاطع ص ۷۸۰ ذیل «خوار» همین زنجیره را می‌آورد: «اوستا xᵛāθra- (رفاه، آسایش)، پهلوی xᵛār، کردی xār، افغانی xwār، بلوچی xwār، طبری xār». پس ادعای نورایی در این گره درست است؛ و یادداشت خودِ نمودار را باید وارونه خواند: آنچه اینجا رسم شده همان ریشه‌شناسی پذیرفتهٔ همگانی است.

entries.note: Pokorny p.344: 'Root/lemma: eti | Meaning: out; further, etc.' with Skt. áti, Av. aiti-, OP atiy- 'over-, back-', Gk. ἔτι, Gaul. eti, Lat. et / etiam, Goth. iþ and prefix id-, OE/OS ed-, ON ið-, OHG et-/it- 'again'. Watkins/AHD prints the lemma with Nourai's exact wording: 'eti. Above, beyond. 1. Germanic *ith- in Old Norse idha, whirlpool: EDDY. 2. Latin et, and (< “furthermore”): ET CETERA. [Pok. eti 344.]' — so the whole chart (root gloss, the two branches, and the two English words) is copied straight out of the AHD appendix, and it is right. Modern handbooks keep the root: De Vaan/Beekes/Derksen reconstruct *h₁eti (an old locative of *h₁et-), Ringe simply *éti, with descendants PIE > PII *áti, Proto-Italic *et, Proto-Germanic *idi, Gk. ἔτι, PCelt. *eti, PBSl. *ati, Toch. B ate.
entries.note_fa: ریشهٔ هندواروپایی آغازین *éti (یا *h₁eti) «فراتر، آن‌سوی؛ و» در پوکورنی ص ۳۴۴ آمده است با شواهد سنسکریت áti، اوستایی aiti-، پارسی باستان atiy-، یونانی ἔτι، لاتینی et و etiam، گوتی iþ و پیشوند id-، انگلیسی باستان ed-، نورس باستان ið-. معنایی که نورایی می‌دهد («بالا، فراتر») عیناً همان است که واتکینز در پیوستِ ریشه‌های هندواروپایی فرهنگ American Heritage آورده، و هر دو شاخهٔ نمودار (لاتینی و ژرمنی) نیز از همان‌جاست. پژوهش امروزی (دِوان، بیکس، درکسن) آن را *h₁eti، صورتِ حالت مکانیِ کهنِ *h₁et-، بازسازی می‌کند. ادعای نورایی درست است.

nodes.derivation: Av. aiti- is the Avestan continuant of PIE *éti, used as a preverb/prefix 'over, beyond, across' (Skt. áti is its exact match). Kent's Old Persian lexicon, p.166, gives it under the Old Persian entry: 'ati-, prefix, "beyond, across": Av. aiti, Skt. áti, Gk. ἔτι "yet, longer", Lt. et "and", pIE *eti'. Klein s.v. et likewise cites 'Avestic aiti, "over, beyond"' — which is where Nourai's gloss comes from word for word. Phonologically PIE *e > Indo-Iranian *a and the *-i is preserved; Avestan writes ai- for a- before a following palatal element, hence aiti beside Skt. áti. The '1' in 'aiti 1' is Nourai's homograph number, distinguishing this particle from other aiti- entries in his book.

nodes.derivation: Latin et 'and' continues *éti; the semantic step is 'furthermore, moreover' > 'and', exactly as Pokorny puts it ('Latin et "and also", Paelignian Umbrian et, Latin etiam "and, also, still", Gaulish eti "also, further", eti-c "and also" (*eti-kʷe)'). Klein's entry is the reference Nourai cites and says the same. Nourai's second item 'et-cě-terî' is the phrase et cētera analysed into its parts: et + cēterī, and cēterus is itself *ke-etero- = the deictic particle *ke- (his cross-reference 'Ki 2') plus the comparative *etero- 'the other of two' (his 'I 2'). Watkins agrees, filing ET CETERA under both eti and ko-: 'Preposed in *ke-etero- (*e-tero-, a second time, again; see i-) in Latin cēterus (neuter plural cētera), the other part, that which remains: ET CETERA.' Etymonline: 'from Latin et cetera, literally "and the others", from et "and" + neuter plural of ceterus … from Proto-Italic *ke-etero-'. The gloss ':and other things' is Klein's ('et cetera, "and other things"').
nodes.derivation_fa: لاتینی et «و» دنبالهٔ همان *éti است؛ تحوّل معنایی از «افزون بر این، وانگهی» به «و» رفته است — چنان‌که پوکورنی می‌نویسد و لاتینی etiam «و نیز» و گالی eti-c «و همچنین» (< *eti-kʷe) را نیز کنار آن می‌آورد. جزء دوم نمودار، «et-cě-terî»، همان عبارت et cētera است که نورایی به اجزایش تجزیه کرده: et + cēterī، و خودِ cēterus از *ke-etero- است، یعنی جزء اشارهٔ *ke- (ارجاع او به Ki 2) به‌اضافهٔ *etero- «آن دیگری از میان دو تا» (ارجاع او به I 2). واتکینز و اتیمانلاین همین تحلیل را دارند. ادعای نورایی درست است.

nodes.derivation: Nourai's 'ith' is the Germanic reflex of *éti as Klein and Watkins write it (*ith-), seen in Gothic iþ 'and, but, however' and in the productive prefix Gothic id-, OE/OS ed-, ON ið-, OHG et-/it- 'again, back' (OE id-witan 'reproach', OHG ita-, itwīz). The chart's four-part gloss 'back, again, water flowing back, whirlpool' is Klein's own wording at eddy, where he explains ON iða as 'lit. meaning "that which rebounds or flows back", fr. ON pref. ið- "again"' — so 'water flowing back, whirlpool' is not a Germanic *ith- meaning but the meaning of the ON derivative iða; Nourai has folded the derivative's sense into the base word. Modern reconstruction writes the base *idi/*idi- (Proto-Germanic), with the noun ON iða f. 'eddy'. Etymonline: Old Norse iða 'whirlpool', from Proto-Germanic *ith- 'a second time, again'. Substantively the node is right; only the gloss is compressed.

nodes.derivation: Eddy: Middle English (Scottish) ydy, mid-15c., almost certainly from Old Norse iða 'whirlpool' — a Norse loan into northern English/Scots, hence the initial e-/y- variation; Klein: 'eddy, n., whirlpool; current of air. — ME. ydy, prob. fr. ON. iða, "whirlpool", lit. "that which rebounds or flows back"'. Etymonline says the same: 'mid-15c., Scottish ydy, possibly related to Old Norse iða "whirlpool," from Proto-Germanic *ith- "a second time, again"'. 'Eddy current' is not an old word but a 19th-century physics compound (the induced circulating currents in a conductor, also called Foucault currents), formed inside English on eddy; Nourai lists it, as AHD-style lists do, as a derivative rather than a separate etymon.

nodes.derivation: The Avestan word is ūna- 'insufficient, deficient, scanty' (Bartholomae: 'ungenügend, mangelhaft', and 'geringfügig, kärglich'), from zero-grade *uH-no-/*u-no- of the root, i.e. the same participial *-no- formation as Skt. ūná- 'wanting, less by', Gothic wans, Arm. unayn. Beside it stands the middle present participle uyamna- 'lacking' to a present stem u-ya-, with the negated compound an-uyamna- 'not defective, complete' (Vr.15.1: 'uyamna anuyamnāiš daste' — 'so that what is defective is made complete'). Nourai's three shapes are that pair plus, in 'unâ', the Sanskrit match ūná- that Pokorny prints immediately before the Avestan form. Pokorny 345: 'Old Indic ūna-, Avestan ūna- "insufficient, inadequate, lack, be short of", Avestan uyamna- ds. (participle present Med. to present u-ya-)'; Klein p.1687 s.v. vain: 'cogn. with OI. ūnaḥ "insufficient, wanting", Avestic ūna-, "wanting"'.

nodes.derivation: The word itself is well attested: Borhān-e Qāteʿ p.2293 s.v. ونگ gives 'بمعنی تهی و خالی، و کنایه از تهی‌دستی باشد، و درویش و گدا و مفلس را نیز گویند', and Moʿin's Farhang has the same two entries ('ونگ vang (ص.) تهی، خالی' / 'ونگ (ص.) درویش، تهیدست، مفلس، سایل'). The ETYMOLOGY is the disputed part, and Nourai's own note is accurate. Horn no.1085 (p.243) set up 'veng, ving "leer; arm"' beside Av. ūna-, Skt. ūná-, Arm. unain, Goth. wans, Gk. εὖνις, crediting the idea to Nöldeke and himself refusing Nöldeke's further comparison with Latin vānus; Pokorny took it over and printed 'npers. (*gvang) vang "empty, bare, lacking, poor, needy"' on p.345 — note the starred *gvang, which shows he had to posit an unattested initial to get New Persian v- out of PIE *u-. Hübschmann, Persische Studien p.105, commenting on Horn's no.1085, says only 'Unsicher.' Moʿin's footnote to the Borhān entry repeats exactly this history — 'هرن veng, ving را بمعنی خالی و فقیر ضبط کرده و وجه اشتقاقی برای آن نوشته است … ولی هوبشمان آنرا قطعی نمی‌داند' — and adds his own verdict, 'درست بنظر نمی‌رسد' ('it does not look right'). The obstacles are that there is no Middle Persian *wang, that NP و- from an Old Iranian vowel-initial *u- is irregular, and that Persian ونگ elsewhere is a noise word (= بانگ). So: accepted by Horn and Pokorny, doubted by Hübschmann, rejected by Moʿin — 'plausible', and Nourai's flagging of HUB:105 is exactly right.

nodes.derivation: All three are the Latin members of the family as Watkins arranges them: vānus 'empty, vain' < suffixed *wā-no-; vacāre 'to be empty' < extended *wak- (with the archaic doublet vocāre/vocuus that Plautus puns on); vāstus 'empty, desolate' < extended and suffixed *wās-to-, whence vāstāre 'lay waste'. Ernout–Meillet make the same three-way link twice over: s.v. uānus 'Pour l'étymologie, v. uacāre et uastus', and s.v. uacō 'en latin même, cf. uānus et uastus; hors du latin, cf. v.isl. vanr "manquant", skr. ūna- = av. ūna- "qui manque de, incomplet", arm. unayn "vide", gr. εὖνις'. Pokorny is more reserved than Nourai's 'AHD' source: he calls vānus 'perhaps here' and vacō 'very dubious (because the k-extension is attested only in Italic)', while vāstus he treats as certainly related (*u̯āsto-s, = OIr. fás 'empty', OHG wuosti 'waste'). Nourai follows AHD, which is the mainstream position.

nodes.derivation: Exactly Watkins's list of English reflexes under eu-2. Routes: (a) WASTE is not a direct Latin borrowing — Latin vāstāre/vāstus passed into Gallo-Romance and was altered under Frankish *wōstjan to Old North French / Anglo-French wast(e), waster (central Old French gaster, Modern French gâter), whence Middle English wasten c.1200 'devastate, ravage'; the initial w- is the Germanic-influenced Norman form (Etymonline). (b) vacāre gives vacate (1640s, from vacātus), vacuum (1550s, Latin neuter of vacuus), vacation (late 14c. via Old French), and, through Vulgar Latin *vocitus > Old French voide/vuide, void and its compound avoid (Anglo-French avoider 'to empty out'). (c) vānus gives vain (c.1300, Old French vain), vanity (c.1200, Old French vanité < Latin vānitātem), and vanish (early 14c., Old French esvanir < Vulgar Latin *exvānīre for Latin ēvānēscere). All three sub-lists are Watkins's, unchanged.

nodes.derivation: Nourai's 'wanatôn' is Watkins's North Germanic *wanatōn 'to lack', a denominative verb built on the Germanic adjective *wanaz 'lacking' (Gothic wans, ON vanr, OE/OS/OFris. wan, OHG wan), itself the *wo-no-/*u-ono- form of the root — Pokorny 345: 'Gothic (*gwans) wans "lacking, missing, wanting" (*u-ono-s or *uə-no-s); Old Icelandic van-r, Old Frisian Old English Old Saxon Old High German wan ds.' nodes.derivation: English want is a Norse loan of the Scandinavian settlement period, first recorded c.1200 as wanten 'be lacking, be deficient in something', from Old Norse vanta 'to lack' (earlier *wanaton), i.e. it did not descend through Old English but was borrowed from Old Norse — which is why it has no Old English ancestor beside cognate wanian 'to diminish' (> wane). The modern dominant sense 'desire, wish for, feel the need of' is a late semantic shift, first recorded 1706 (Etymonline); the noun want 'deficiency' is equally c.1200, matching ON vant, neuter of vanr. Skeat's entry gives the same route from the Icelandic adjective vanr.
